title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier (with at most one automated repair) increases the fraction of intent‑driven configuration proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Each pair evaluated a single shared_initial candidate under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation and ≤1 automated repair). Results: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and model, single‑shot generation was near ceiling, limiting observable marginal rescue by the guarded pipeline. All preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts are archived with the study id to support replication and follow‑up experiments that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, or repair budget.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being actively applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. Operators require semantic guarantees—sequencing, reachability, and policy preservation—that cannot be assessed by syntax alone. Consequently, hybrid architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) have been proposed to reduce operational risk. However, the practical benefit of such architectures depends on how the estimand is defined (what is held fixed), the generator's single‑shot quality, the validator's expressiveness, and the allowed repair budget.

We preregistered a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) to quantify the deterministic rescue utility provided by a validator plus at most one automated repair when the same single LLM candidate is evaluated under two treatments. For each intent the system generated one shared_initial candidate using gpt-5-mini and compared: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate without repair, and (b) guarded — run deterministic validation and allow at most one automated repair that is itself re‑validated. The core research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same single candidate without repair?

We report a fully archived confirmatory run of 300 paired intents stratified by difficulty. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation isolating deterministic rescue utility under a shared_initial estimand; (2) a complete execution and analysis bundle including validator traces and the single automated repair transcript archived with the run; and (3) an artifact‑grounded interpretation of estimator conditioning, ceiling effects, and operational implications for NetOps pipelines. We note explicitly that the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation was not executed and no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed. We further emphasize that the shared_initial estimand conditions on a single LLM draw per intent and therefore excludes any verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (for example, resampling or iterative candidate generation).
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and systems work document extensive activity at the intersection of LLMs and NetOps, covering intent‑based translation, configuration synthesis, repair, and tool‑augmented agentic frameworks. Prior work reports generate→validate→repair architectures and planner‑centric tool orchestration that call external validators to improve correctness. Empirical systems papers report improved syntactic and semantic correctness with validator assistance, although success rates depend strongly on task definitions, validator coverage, and candidate generation strategies [W4416927413; W4411015066; W4404240614]. Surveys and practitioner studies also emphasize operator skepticism about deployability despite high syntactic correctness in controlled experiments [W7167855398; W4416927413].

Two methodological gaps motivated our design. First, many prior comparisons conflate validator rescue with benefits from drawing additional independent model candidates: permitting resampling mixes estimator effects (generation variance) with deterministic validator effects. Second, standardized public benchmarks that emphasize semantic correctness (reachability, policy compliance) are limited; available datasets often differ in scope and validator expressiveness. We position our experiment to address the first gap by conditioning on a single shared_initial candidate per intent, thereby quantifying only the deterministic recovery achievable without additional independent model draws. This isolates the validator/repair mechanism from sampling effects of the generator, a distinction of operational relevance when a policy constrains organizations to single model calls per change request.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration fixed the primary estimand: the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded minus baseline) computed on paired cases that evaluate the same shared_initial candidate. The confirmatory design required 300 analyzable pairs (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high), explicit inclusion/exclusion rules, an analysis executor producing exact paired inference, and deterministic artifact logging. The preregistration also described an optional pilot (n = 60) for discordance estimation; that pilot was not executed and no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed — this decision and its implications are reported here.

Task generation and synthetic suite. Tasks were produced deterministically by the repository task generator into a synthetic_topology_suite and stratified by generator metadata into low, medium, and high difficulty bins based on changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, and required_command_count. The task manifest records required_sequences and intent constraints for each item; representative patterns include 'shutdown_configure_restore' (medium) and 'paired_link_atomic_mtu_change' (hard). The synthetic suite enforces protected interfaces and preserve_unspecified_state invariants that the validator checks. Six representative tasks and their shared_initial responses are included in the archived run bundle to illustrate typical difficulty patterns and validator diagnostics.

Modeling, shared_initial protocol, and orchestration. The declared model for generation was gpt-5-mini. To implement the shared_initial estimand, the pipeline produced a single shared_initial generation per pair and reused that identical candidate for both conditions. The guarded pipeline executed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on the shared_initial candidate and, if flagged, invoked at most one automated repair attempt (repair budget ≤1) which produced an edited candidate subject to a final deterministic revalidation. The baseline pipeline accepted the same shared_initial candidate unmodified. This design isolates deterministic validator/repair rescue from benefits that would accrue by drawing additional independent generator candidates or steering the generator interactively.

Validator, scoring rule, and repair policy. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule: deterministic checks for required sequencing (must_be_down_for_fields), required_command_count, preservation of unspecified state, reachability invariants encoded in the synthetic topology, and forbidden‑template protections (protected_interfaces). Scoring is binary: unflagged==pass; flagged after allowed repair==failure for the primary estimand. The automated repair routine is a constrained edit operator that attempts localized corrections (e.g., insert missing sequencing commands or reorder required operations) and logs a repair provider trace. All validation decisions and repair provider traces were archived. Repair use was limited (≤1 invocation per pair) by design to measure bounded automated rescue.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and data integrity. The hosted adapter completed the confirmatory run with completed_episode_count = 600 and complete_pair_count = 300; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared_initial generations plus one repair call). Deterministic auditing recorded stage_counts showing 300 shared_initial_generation events and 1 repair event. No provider outages, failed episodes, or unscorable episodes were observed according to the preregistered missingness rules; the missingness summary records zeros for failed or unscorable episodes. The contamination summary is empty. Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode accounting and provider call audit totals across stages.

Marginal and paired outcomes. Condition summary: baseline successes = 299/300 (0.9966666667), guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1 (guarded‑only), n01 = 0 (baseline‑only), n00 = 0. The preregistered confirmatory analysis (exact McNemar two‑sided) returned p = 1.0; absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with B = 10000 resamples and seed = 1729 yields [0.00, 0.01]. Per‑stratum counts: low = 100/100 baseline & guarded; medium = 100/100 baseline & guarded; high = baseline 99/100 vs guarded 100/100.

Rescue diagnostic and repair transcript summary. The single discordant episode (n10 = 1) triggered the permitted automated repair. Validator traces attribute the initial flag to an omitted sequencing command required by the intent (a must_be_down_for_fields violation): the shared_initial candidate lacked an 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change. The automated repair inserted the missing sequencing command; the deterministic validator then reported valid == true for the repaired candidate. The low‑level repair provider trace and the full validator trace for this episode are archived in the run bundle; in the Results we provide the concise semantic summary above rather than reproducing verbatim provider transcripts.

Statistical interpretation. The baseline single‑shot success near ceiling produced only one discordant pair and therefore constrained inferential sensitivity: the exact test p‑value of 1.0 reflects the paucity of discordant evidence under the shared_initial estimand. The bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute paired improvement at ≤1 percentage point in this experimental context. These results should not be taken as demonstrating equivalence of strategies under alternative estimand choices — for example, permitting independent resampling, iterative generation, or verifier‑guided steering could increase rescue opportunities materially and must be evaluated under those alternative estimands.
sections.discussion:
Operational meaning of the shared_initial estimand. Conditioning on a single LLM draw corresponds to operational policies in which organizations limit model calls per change request (e.g., cost, latency, or process constraints). Under that policy the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validator and bounded repair rescue applied to the same candidate. By contrast, operational workflows that allow resampling, search, or verifier‑directed candidate selection change the estimand and typically increase the achievable success rates because they exploit generator variance. Teams should choose an estimand aligned to their operational constraints when evaluating pipelines.

Ceiling effects, pilot decisions, and power. The preregistered power target assumed baseline discordance sufficient to detect a 10 percentage‑point absolute improvement with reasonable power. Because the optional pilot for discordance estimation was not executed, the main run encountered a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) and consequently low discordance (m = 1), limiting statistical sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. We recommend future confirmatory designs run a small pilot under the target sampling frame to estimate discordance before fixing confirmatory N or otherwise predefine alternative estimands that increase sensitivity (e.g., allow resampling or expand repair budget).

Validator expressiveness and failure‑mode dependence. The observed dominant failure mode was a sequencing omission; other potential failure classes (reachability violations, unintended removal of protected ACLs, or forbidden‑template modifications) were not observed at scale on this synthetic suite. The marginal value of a guarded pipeline therefore depends on the failure‑mode distribution in the deployment population and on the validator's encoded invariants. A richer validator or different task distribution could increase the observed rescue rate.

Practical recommendations. If production policy constrains single model calls, adding deterministic validation and a bounded automated repair can correct localized sequencing omissions (as observed here). If operational tolerance permits additional model calls, organizations should evaluate resampling or verifier‑guided generation as a distinct estimand because these strategies may provide larger gains. For higher assurance, expand repair budgets, permit iterative repair cycles, or employ stronger domain‑adapted generators and higher‑coverage validators.

Reproducibility and artifact grounding. All preregistration documents, task manifests, model configuration, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, analysis CSVs (condition summary and paired contingency table), deterministic reconciliation, and analysis logs are archived under the study id in the run bundle. Analysis parameters (bootstrap resamples = 10000, seed = 1729) and exact executor outputs are recorded. Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode accounting and provider call audits. The archived run bundle contains the low‑level repair provider trace for the single repaired episode; the body reports a concise semantic summary of that repair while the full trace is available in the artifacts for forensic inspection. These artifacts permit independent recomputation of the reported contingency counts and bootstrap CI with a deterministic executor.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). Under the tested synthetic suite and bounded repair budget, deterministic validator+repair rescued a single sequencing omission. The near‑ceiling baseline limits inferential sensitivity to small absolute improvements under the shared_initial estimand. We release the preregistration, execution and analysis artifacts, representative task manifests, and validator traces in the archived run bundle to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary estimand choice, model strength, topology realism, or repair strategies.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
